items.title: Foundation of the Empire & Chandragupta Maurya
items.body:
## Birth of the Mauryan Empire

- The **Mauryan Empire began in 322 BCE** when **Chandragupta Maurya** overthrew the **Nanda dynasty** (its last ruler **Dhanananda**), guided by his mentor **Chanakya (Kautilya / Vishnugupta)**.
- His origins are debated: **Brahmanical tradition** calls him born of a **shudra woman** in the Nanda court; **Buddhist tradition** links him to a **Kshatriya clan (the Mauryas)** of the **Gorakhpur** region.
- **Political unity was achieved for the first time in Indian history** under the Mauryas, and **monarchy** replaced the older republic/oligarchy forms.

## Expansion & Extent

- After defeating the Greek **Seleucus I in 305 BCE**, Chandragupta gained **Afghanistan, Baluchistan and areas west of the Indus** — in return he gave **500 war elephants**.
- The empire covered **Bihar, Orissa, Bengal** and the **north/north-west**; only **Kerala, Tamil Nadu and parts of the North-East** stayed outside Mauryan rule.
- An **autocrat** who kept all power in his hands, he maintained a huge army — **Pliny** records **600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants**.
- Capital: **Pataliputra** (modern **Patna**), at the confluence of major trade routes.

figure.alt: Map showing the extent of the Mauryan Empire under Chandragupta or Bindusara before 273 BCE
figure.caption: Extent of the empire under Chandragupta / Bindusara (before 273 BCE), reaching Kandahar in the north-west with Pataliputra as capital.

keyPoints: Mauryan Empire founded in 322 BCE by Chandragupta Maurya, who overthrew the Nanda ruler Dhanananda with Chanakya's help.
Defeated Seleucus I in 305 BCE, gaining Afghanistan/Baluchistan/west-of-Indus in exchange for 500 elephants.
Achieved the first political unification of India; monarchy replaced republics/oligarchies.
Kerala, Tamil Nadu and parts of the North-East remained outside Mauryan rule.
Pliny records his army as 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants.
items.mnemonic: Ruler order 'CBA' = Chandragupta → Bindusara → Ashoka (the three peak Mauryas).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Major Facts; Chandragupta Maurya)

items.title: Chanakya (Kautilya) & the Arthashastra
items.body:
## Chanakya — Architect of the Empire

- **Chanakya**, also called **Kautilya** and **Vishnugupta**, was the **contemporary and mentor** of Chandragupta Maurya and guided the overthrow of the Nandas.
- He continued as **prime minister** into the reign of **Bindusara**.

## The Arthashastra

- Written by **Kautilya in Sanskrit**; it is the **most important source** for the Mauryan Empire.
- Contains **15 books and 180 chapters**, grouped into **3 broad divisions**, covering the entire **legal and bureaucratic framework** of governance, economics and military strategy.
- Stresses the king's duty to promote the **welfare (Yogakshema)** of subjects — through law and order plus **agricultural productivity, irrigation, fair taxation and disaster relief**.
- Though **compiled a few centuries after** Maurya rule, it preserves **authentic information** about Mauryan administration.
keyPoints: Chanakya = Kautilya = Vishnugupta; mentor of Chandragupta and prime minister continuing under Bindusara.
Arthashastra was written by Kautilya in Sanskrit — the single most important source on the Mauryas.
Structure: 15 books, 180 chapters, 3 broad divisions.
Emphasises the king's duty of Yogakshema (welfare) via irrigation, fair taxation and disaster relief.
Compiled centuries later but contains authentic administrative detail.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Literary Sources — Arthashastra)

items.title: Megasthenes' Indica & Literary Sources
items.body:
## Megasthenes & Indica

- **Megasthenes** was the **Greek ambassador** sent by **Seleucus** to **Chandragupta Maurya's court**, living at **Pataliputra**.
- He documented Mauryan society, administration and the capital in **Indica**; the original is lost and survives only as **fragments compiled by later Greek writers**.

## Other Literary Sources

- **Arthashastra** (Kautilya) — the foremost administrative source.
- **Mudrarakshasa** — a Sanskrit drama by **Vishakhadatta** (Gupta era) dramatising **Chandragupta's victory over the Nandas** under Kautilya's guidance; reflects socio-economic conditions.
- **Buddhist literature and the Puranas** add further accounts of the empire.
keyPoints: Megasthenes was Seleucus's ambassador to Chandragupta's court at Pataliputra.
He wrote Indica; the original is lost and survives only as fragments in later Greek writers.
Mudrarakshasa (Vishakhadatta, Gupta era) dramatises Chandragupta's defeat of the Nandas under Kautilya.
Buddhist texts and the Puranas supplement the sources.
Together with the Arthashastra, Indica is a key window into Mauryan administration.
items.mnemonic: Two pillars of Mauryan sources — 'A & I': Arthashastra (insider Kautilya) + Indica (outsider Megasthenes).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Literary Sources — Indica, Mudrarakshasa)

items.title: Bindusara (297–272/268 BCE)
items.body:
## Bindusara — The Southern Expansion

- **Son and successor of Chandragupta Maurya**, he took the throne in **297 BCE**.
- The Greeks called him **Amitragata / Amitrochates / Allitrochates**, meaning **'slayer of enemies'**.
- He **extended the empire southward**, bringing **sixteen states** under Mauryan control and conquering much of the **Indian peninsula**.
- Apart from the far south, the only kingdom outside his control was **Kalinga** (later conquered under Ashoka).
- His reign maintained **continued links with the Greeks**, and **Kautilya continued as prime minister**.
keyPoints: Bindusara, son of Chandragupta, ascended in 297 BCE.
Greeks called him Amitragata / Amitrochates — 'slayer of enemies'.
Extended the empire south, subduing sixteen states across the peninsula.
Kalinga remained unconquered until Ashoka's reign.
Kautilya continued as prime minister; Greek links were maintained.
items.mnemonic: Bindusara = 'Amitraghata, the enemy-slayer' — he slew 16 states but not Kalinga.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Bindusara)

items.title: Ashoka — Accession & Inscriptions
items.body:
## Ashoka the Great

- **Son of Bindusara** and grandson of Chandragupta, he ascended the throne around **268 BCE** (genealogy: 272/268 BCE) and is counted among the greatest kings of the subcontinent.
- He was the **first ruler to maintain direct contact with his people** through **inscriptions**.

## The Inscriptions

- **Ashokan inscriptions number 39**, classified as **Major Rock Edicts, Minor Rock Edicts, Separate Rock Edicts, Major Pillar Edicts and Minor Pillar Edicts**.
- His **personal name 'Ashoka'** appears only in the **Maski Edict** and in copies of **Minor Rock Edict I** (three sites in Karnataka, one in Madhya Pradesh); all others call him **'Devanampiya Piyadasi'** (Beloved-of-the-Gods).
- Stone **pillars were quarried at Chunar near Varanasi** and transported across India; each pillar is a **single piece of buff-coloured sandstone**.
- Inscriptions are found in **India, Nepal, Pakistan and Afghanistan**, usually placed on **ancient highways**.
- Contemporary rulers named include **Antiochus II (Syria), Ptolemy II (Egypt), Antigonus (Macedonia), Magas (Cyrene) and Alexander (Epirus)**.
keyPoints: Ashoka, son of Bindusara, ascended c. 268 BCE (272/268); first Indian ruler to speak to his people via inscriptions.
39 inscriptions: Major/Minor Rock, Separate Rock, Major/Minor Pillar edicts.
Name 'Ashoka' appears only in the Maski Edict and Minor Rock Edict I; elsewhere he is 'Devanampiya Piyadasi'.
Pillars quarried at Chunar (near Varanasi); each is a single piece of buff sandstone.
Edicts found in India, Nepal, Pakistan and Afghanistan, placed along ancient highways.
Kanganahalli (Sannati, Karnataka) yielded the 'Ranyo Ashoka' portrait-inscription of the emperor.
items.mnemonic: Ashoka's name-clue — 'MASKI unmasks Ashoka' (only Maski/Minor Rock Edict I give his real name).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Ashoka; inscriptions)

figure.alt: Schematic map of the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka
figure.caption: Capital Pataliputra; Taxila (NW), Ujjain, Kalinga (261 BCE war), Suvarnagiri (south).

items.title: The Kalinga War (261 BCE) & Its Impact
items.body:
## The Turning Point

- The **Kalinga War of 261 BCE** caused enormous loss of life and **profoundly changed Ashoka's outlook** towards violence and war.
- The **Thirteenth Major Rock Edict** describes the Kalinga war and Ashoka's remorse; the **Kalinga (Separate) Edict** proclaims **'All men are my children.'**
- After the war Ashoka **embraced Buddhism** and promoted **peace and non-violence**.

## Consequences

- Policy shifted from **Bherighosha (sound of the war-drum)** to **Dhammaghosha (sound of dhamma)** — from **physical conquest to cultural conquest**.
- **State policy was framed on Buddhist principles**; foreign lands were to be won **ideologically**, not militarily.
- He sent **ambassadors of peace** to Greece and West Asia, and his children **Mahendra (Mahinda) and Sanghamitra to Ceylon (Sri Lanka)**.
keyPoints: Kalinga War fought in 261 BCE; its bloodshed transformed Ashoka.
13th Major Rock Edict records the Kalinga war; the Kalinga Edict declares 'All men are my children'.
Shift from Bherighosha (war-drum) to Dhammaghosha (dhamma) — physical to cultural conquest.
Ashoka embraced Buddhism and promoted non-violence.
Sent his children Mahendra (Mahinda) and Sanghamitra to Ceylon/Sri Lanka.
items.mnemonic: Kalinga aftermath = 'Bheri to Dhamma' — the war-drum (Bherighosha) falls silent for the drum of dhamma (Dhammaghosha).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Impact of the Kalinga War)

items.title: Ashoka's Dhamma & Internal Policy
items.body:
## The Concept of Dhamma

- Ashoka initiated **Dhamma**, emphasising **moral governance, social welfare and respect for all living beings**.
- He set the ideal of **paternal kingship** — the king regarding his **subjects as his children**.
- His teachings aimed to **strengthen the family and the existing social order**, and were promoted among all social groups, **including women**.

## Officers of Dhamma & Governance

- He appointed **Dhamma Mahamatras** to propagate dharma and ensure the **material well-being** of the common folk.
- He appointed **Rajukas**, officers empowered **both to reward and to punish** people for violations of established rules.
- He instructed the **mahamatras not to torture people without due cause**, reflecting his welfare-oriented rule.
keyPoints: Dhamma stressed moral governance, social welfare and respect for all life.
Ashoka set the ideal of paternal kingship — subjects treated as his children.
Dhamma Mahamatras propagated dharma and looked after people's material well-being.
Rajukas were empowered both to reward and to punish.
Teachings targeted all groups including women and reinforced the family/social order.
items.mnemonic: Dhamma officers — 'Mahamatras Mind morals, Rajukas Reward & Rebuke.'
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Dhamma; Internal policy of Ashoka)

items.title: The Edicts of Ashoka — Rock & Pillar Edicts
items.body:
## Major Rock Edicts

- The **Major Edicts of Ashoka** are a set of **14 detailed rock inscriptions**.
- Key contents:
  - **First Rock Edict** — prohibition of **animal sacrifices**.
  - **Fourth Rock Edict** — **Bherighosha replaced by Dhammaghosha**.
  - **Fifth Rock Edict** — **appointment of Dhamma Mahamatras**.
  - **Thirteenth Rock Edict** — describes the **Kalinga War (261 BCE)**.

## Pillar Edicts & Special Inscriptions

- **Pillar Edict V** — lists **animals and birds not to be killed** and records the **release of 25 prisoners**.
- **Pillar Edict VI** — deals with the **Dhamma Policy**.
- **Rummindei Inscription (Nepal)** — commemorates the **Buddha's birthplace**; Ashoka visited **Lumbini**.
- **Kalinga Edict** — **'All men are my children.'**
- **Saugara (Sohgaura) Copper Plate** — **famine-relief measures in Magadha**.
- **Brahmagiri Minor Rock Edicts I & II** — deal with **local administration**.
- The **Ashoka Chakra** depicts the **Dharma Chakra**; its **24 spokes** represent the causal links taught by the Buddha.
keyPoints: Major Edicts = 14 rock inscriptions.
1st RE: bans animal sacrifice; 4th RE: Bherighosha → Dhammaghosha; 5th RE: appoints Dhamma Mahamatras; 13th RE: Kalinga War.
Pillar Edict V: animals not to be killed + release of 25 prisoners; Pillar Edict VI: Dhamma policy.
Rummindei (Nepal) marks the Buddha's birthplace (Lumbini); Saugara copper plate records famine relief.
Ashoka Chakra = Dharma Chakra with 24 spokes.
Erragudi (Yerragudi) in Andhra Pradesh bears Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts — a key AP Ashokan site.
items.mnemonic: Rock Edicts '1-4-5-13' = Sacrifice-ban, Drum-swap, Mahamatras, Kalinga.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Edicts table; Major Facts)

items.title: Languages & Scripts of the Edicts
items.body:
## Languages of Ashoka's Edicts

- The languages used were **Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic**.

## Scripts by Region

- Across most of the subcontinent the edicts are in **Prakrit written in the Brahmi script**.
- In the **north-west**, they are in the **Aramaic language and Kharoshthi script** — the **Shahbazgarhi and Manshera** edicts are in **Kharoshthi**.
- In **Afghanistan**, edicts appear in **both Aramaic and Greek**.
keyPoints: Languages of the edicts: Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic.
Most of India: Prakrit language in Brahmi script.
North-west: Aramaic language, Kharoshthi script (Shahbazgarhi and Manshera).
Afghanistan: both Aramaic and Greek.
Brahmi is the dominant script; Kharoshthi is confined to the north-west.
items.mnemonic: Scripts by direction — 'Brahmi Broadly, Kharoshthi in the (north-)West'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (languages/scripts of edicts)

items.title: Ashoka & the Spread of Buddhism
items.body:
## Patron of Buddhism

- Ashoka became a **major patron of Buddhism**, helping spread it across **Asia, including Sri Lanka**.
- The **Third Buddhist Council** was held under his patronage in **250 BC at Pataliputra**, presided over by **Mogaliputta Tissa**, to **purify Buddhism** of corrupt and opportunistic factions in the Sangha.

## Missionary Activity

- He dispatched missionaries — including his son **Mahinda (Mahendra)** and daughter **Sanghamitra** — to **Ceylon (Sri Lanka)**, and others to **Burma** and beyond.
- Because of this, Ashoka is regarded as the **First Global Ambassador of India**, building cultural contact between the developed Gangetic basin and outlying regions, and between India and the wider world.
keyPoints: Ashoka was a major patron of Buddhism, spreading it across Asia including Sri Lanka.
Third Buddhist Council: 250 BC at Pataliputra, presided by Mogaliputta Tissa.
Council aimed to purify the Sangha of corruption and factions.
Missionaries Mahinda (son) and Sanghamitra (daughter) went to Ceylon; others to Burma.
Ashoka is called the 'First Global Ambassador of India'.
The Third Buddhist Council (Pataliputra) was convened under Ashoka and presided over by Moggaliputta Tissa.
items.mnemonic: 3rd Council = '3 P's' — Pataliputra, Presided by Mogaliputta Tissa, to Purify the Sangha.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (spread of Buddhism; Third Buddhist Council)

items.title: Mauryan Central Administration
items.body:
## An Autocratic, Council-Aided Monarchy

- The administration was **autocratic** — powers concentrated in the ruler — yet the king was **assisted by a council whose advice was not binding**; high officers were chosen from the councillors.
- Our knowledge comes chiefly from **Megasthenes' Indica** and **Kautilya's Arthashastra**.

## The High Functionaries (tirthas)

- **Mantrin** — minister; **Purohita** — highest priest; **Senapati** — commander-in-chief; **Yuvaraja** — crown prince.

## Key Officials (Arthashastra)

- **Samaharta** — collector-general of revenue (highest officer of assessment).
- **Sannidhata (Samnidhata)** — chief treasury/custodian of the state treasury and storehouse.
- **Vyavaharika (Dharmastha)** — chief justice of the **civil court**.
- **Pradeshta** — chief justice of the **criminal court (Kantakashodhan)**.
- **Dhamma Mahamatra** — post created by Ashoka for propagating Dhamma.
- The state ran an **elaborate system of espionage (spies)** underpinning the whole machinery.
keyPoints: Autocratic monarchy; king assisted by a council whose advice was non-binding.
Sources: Megasthenes' Indica and Kautilya's Arthashastra.
Tirthas: Mantrin (minister), Purohita (priest), Senapati (C-in-C), Yuvaraja (crown prince).
Samaharta = revenue collector-general/assessment; Sannidhata = chief treasurer.
Vyavaharika = civil court chief justice; Pradeshta = criminal court chief justice; espionage backed the system.
items.mnemonic: Money officers 'SS' — Samaharta collects (assessment), Sannidhata stores (treasury).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Features of administration; functionaries; officials)

items.title: Provincial, Local & Municipal Administration
items.body:
## Provinces

- The empire was **divided into provinces**, each placed **under a prince** and governed with the help of officials.
- Major provinces and capitals:
  - **Uttarapatha → Taxila**; **Dakshinapatha → Suvarnagiri**; **Eastern India → Tosali**; **Avantiratha → Ujjain**; **Kalinga → Tosali/Dhauli**.

## District & Local Officers

- **Rashtrapala / Kumara** — viceroys in charge of a province.
- **Pradesika** — the modern equivalent of a **district magistrate**.
- **Rajukas** — like Patwaris, handled **surveying and land assessment**.
- **Yukta** — subordinate revenue officer; **Sthanika** — collecting officer under the Pradesika; **Gopa** — in charge of **accounts**.

## Pataliputra's Municipal Government (per Megasthenes)

- The capital was administered by **six committees of five members each** — a classic exam fact recorded by **Megasthenes**.
- **Separate arrangements** existed for **rural and urban** administration.

figure.alt: Map of the Maurya Empire showing the capital Pataliputra, provincial cities, edicts of Ashoka and Buddhist sites
figure.caption: The Maurya Empire at its height — capital Pataliputra with provincial centres such as Taxila, Ujjain, Suvarnagiri and Tosali, and sites of Ashoka's edicts.

keyPoints: Empire divided into provinces, each under a prince (Rashtrapala/Kumara as viceroy).
Provincial capitals: Uttarapatha–Taxila, Dakshinapatha–Suvarnagiri, Avantiratha–Ujjain, Kalinga–Tosali/Dhauli.
Pradesika ≈ district magistrate; Rajukas did land survey/assessment; Gopa kept accounts.
Pataliputra was run by six committees of five members each (Megasthenes).
Separate machinery existed for rural and urban administration.
items.mnemonic: Pataliputra municipality = '6 × 5' — six committees, five members each (Megasthenes).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (provinces; officials; Pataliputra administration)

items.title: Economy & Taxation
items.body:
## A State-Controlled Economy

- The **state controlled all economic activity**, brought **new lands under cultivation**, and ran **state farms** worked by **slaves and hired labour** — the Arthashastra notes the striking use of **slaves in agriculture**.
- **27 superintendents (adhyakshas)** regulated the various economic activities of the state.

## Taxation & Revenue

- **Land tax** ranged from **one-fourth to one-sixth of the produce**; in emergencies peasants had to grow more.
- **Samaharta** was the highest officer for **assessment**; **Sannidhata** was the chief custodian of the treasury and storehouse — **assessment was valued more than storage**. Taxes were also collected **in kind**.

## State Monopolies & Currency

- The state held a **monopoly over mining, the sale of liquor and the manufacture of arms**.
- Imperial currency = **punch-marked silver coins** bearing symbols such as the **peacock and hill-crescent**.
keyPoints: State controlled all economic activity; 27 adhyakshas (superintendents) regulated it.
Land tax: one-fourth to one-sixth of produce; extra cultivation demanded in emergencies.
Samaharta headed assessment; Sannidhata kept the treasury/storehouse; taxes also collected in kind.
State monopolies: mining, liquor sale, and manufacture of arms.
Currency: punch-marked silver coins with peacock and hill-crescent symbols.
items.mnemonic: Tax slab '1/4 to 1/6' and monopolies 'MLA' — Mining, Liquor, Arms.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Features of the Economy)

items.title: Art & Architecture
items.body:
## Stone Craft of the Mauryas

- The Mauryans introduced **stone masonry on a wide scale** and achieved **high skill in polishing stone**.
- Each **pillar** was carved from a **single piece of buff-coloured sandstone**.
- The **Lion Capital of Ashoka** (from Sarnath) — the **national emblem of India** — belongs to this era; the **Ashoka Chakra** on it depicts the Dharma Chakra with **24 spokes**.

## Cave Architecture & Notable Examples

- Artisans began **hewing caves from rock for monks** — the earliest being the **Barabar caves near Gaya**; also the **Lomasrishi caves in the Barabar hills**.
- **Ashokan pillar at Lauriya Nandangarh (Bihar)** and the **Bull capital at Rampurva** are important surviving pieces.

figure.alt: A tall polished Ashokan sandstone pillar topped by an animal capital
figure.caption: A monolithic Ashokan pillar with an animal capital (e.g., Lauriya Nandangarh, Bihar) — carved from a single piece of polished buff sandstone.

keyPoints: Mauryans introduced large-scale stone masonry with a distinctive high polish.
Each pillar was a single monolith of buff-coloured sandstone.
The Lion Capital of Ashoka (Sarnath) is India's national emblem; its chakra has 24 spokes.
Earliest rock-cut caves: Barabar caves near Gaya (also Lomasrishi caves).
Notable pieces: Ashokan pillar at Lauriya Nandangarh and the Bull capital at Rampurva.
items.mnemonic: Mauryan art 'PPC' — Polished Pillars (single sandstone), and rock-cut Caves at Barabar.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Art and Architecture; cultural elements)

items.title: Society & Material Culture
items.body:
## Spread of Material Culture

- Mauryan conquest **opened the doors to trade and missionary activity**, spreading material culture beyond the Gangetic core.
- The material culture rested on the **intensive use of iron**, the **prevalence of writing**, abundant **punch-marked coins**, fine **Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW)** pottery, **burnt bricks** and **ring wells**.
- Tools of the age include **socketed axes, sickles and ploughshares**; the **spoked wheel** also came into use.

## Firsts of the Period

- **Burnt bricks** were used for the **first time in north-eastern India** in the Mauryan period.
- **Ring-wells first appeared in the Gangetic plains** during this period.
- Ashoka set a **high ideal of paternal kingship** and strengthened the family and social order.
keyPoints: Mauryan expansion spread material culture via trade and missionaries.
Hallmarks: intensive iron use, writing, punch-marked coins, NBPW pottery, burnt bricks, ring wells.
Tools: socketed axes, sickles, ploughshares; the spoked wheel came into use.
Burnt bricks used for the first time in north-eastern India in this period.
Ring-wells first appeared in the Gangetic plains during Mauryan times.
items.mnemonic: Mauryan material culture 'NBPW + BR' — NBPW pottery, Burnt bricks, Ring-wells.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Spread of material culture)

items.title: Decline & Successors of the Empire
items.body:
## The Fall Begins

- The empire began to **disintegrate after Ashoka's death in 232 BCE**, weakened by feeble successors.
- The last emperor, **Brihadratha**, was **assassinated by his general Pushyamitra Shunga in 180 BCE**, ending the dynasty.
- Later Mauryas (per genealogy): **Dasharatha → Samprati → Shalishuka → Devavarman → Shatadhanvan → Brihadratha**.

## Debated Causes of Decline

1. **Brahmanical reaction** — Ashoka's ban on animal sacrifice hurt the priestly class economically, turning them against him.
2. **Financial crisis** — a huge army and bureaucracy plus lavish grants to Buddhist monks drained the treasury (gold images were later melted).
3. **Oppressive rule** in outlying provinces (e.g., Taxila complaints under Bindusara/Ashoka).
4. **Spread of new knowledge** — material advantages spread out, so the Gangetic core lost its edge; new powers (Shungas, Kanvas, Chetis) arose.
5. **Neglect of the North-West frontier** — leaving passes unguarded before Scythian/Shaka/Greek incursions.
keyPoints: Decline began after Ashoka's death in 232 BCE amid weak successors.
Last emperor Brihadratha was killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga in 180 BCE.
Later Mauryas: Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan, Brihadratha.
Causes: Brahmanical reaction, financial crisis, oppressive provincial rule.
Also: diffusion of material knowledge and neglect of the North-West frontier.
items.mnemonic: Decline causes 'BFONS' — Brahmanical reaction, Financial crisis, Oppression, New knowledge, NW-frontier neglect.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Genealogy; Decline of the Mauryan Empire)
